item.title: Migrating a Legacy Experimentation Engine and its Live DB with Zero Downtime
Data Pipeline Observability
item.description:
The Question

Thousands of data pipelines. Sooner or later, someone has to answer:

For every job, how much data did this run touch, how long did it take, how much did it cost — and how does that compare to yesterday, last week, last month?

Sounds boring. But it’s also the highest-leverage question a platform team can answer: almost every silent pipeline failure shows up first as a change in one of those numbers.


Mapping SRE Golden Signals to Data Pipelines

Google’s SRE framework defines Errors, Traffic, Latency, and Saturation as the foundational metrics for system health.

Signal Data Pipeline Equivalent What It Catches
Errors Task failures & retries Crashes, OOMs
Traffic Rows & bytes (read / written) Volume anomalies, silent drops, and partial writes
Latency Stage & job runtime SLA breaches, data surges, and join skew
Saturation CPU, Memory spill, JVM GC Executor starvation and memory pressure

1) Errors

“the rate of requests that fail.”

In data pipelines, the common trap is relying solely on orchestrator exit codes. A Spark job can exit 0 while hundreds of tasks fail and retry under the hood.

Example metrics:

  • failedTasksCount & taskFailureRate: Categorized by reason (ExceptionFailure, FetchFailed, ExecutorLostFailure).

2) Traffic

“a measure of how much demand is being placed on your system.”

For pipelines, demand is data throughput—rows and bytes in and out, tagged by source, direction, and user.

Example metrics:

  • inputBytesRead & inputRecordsRead: Volume per input scan (S3, Kafka, Delta, Iceberg).
  • outputBytesWritten & outputRecordsWritten: Volume delivered to destination sinks.
  • volumeAnomalyRatio: Run-over-run record count vs. a rolling 7-day baseline.

3) Latency

“the time it takes to service a request,” tracked in percentiles rather than simple averages.

For pipelines, it’s total runtime against business SLAs. But high-level duration only becomes actionable when decomposed.

Example metrics:

  • jobDurationMs & stageDurationMs: Wall-clock runtimes per job and stage.
  • taskSkewRatio (maxTaskDuration / p50TaskDuration): Direct indicator of data skew.

4) Saturation

“how full your service is, emphasizing the resources that are most constrained.”

For Spark, this measures executor CPU, JVM memory, disk I/O, and network limits.

Pipelines rarely fail cold; they saturate first. An executor running out of memory doesn’t crash immediately—it thrashes in GC, spills shuffle partitions to disk before finally throwing an OOM.

Example metrics:

  • jvmGCTime & jvmGCRatio (jvmGCTime / executorRunTime): Time spent in garbage collection. >10% signals severe memory pressure.
  • memorySpillBytes & diskSpillBytes: Shuffle data that couldn’t fit in execution memory and spilled to local disk.
  • executorCpuTime vs executorRunTime: Low ratio indicates tasks blocked on I/O wait (S3 throttling, network shuffle, slow databases).

How to Monitor Across Teams

Take traffic as an example. The two obvious approaches both fail.

Anti-Pattern 1: Cron Queries

The naive answer: running scheduled job SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(<byte_size>) FROM <table> against every table we care about.

  • Doesn’t scale to thousands of tables. Every new table is one more entry to maintain.
  • Costs. Scans entire datasets periodically. That bill isn’t free.
  • Not real-time. By the time the cron queries run, the upstream job finished hours ago.
  • Lack of Attribution. A row count reported doesn’t tell which job produced those rows or what it read to produce them.

Anti-Pattern 2: User-Land Application Hooks

The other obvious answer: push instrumentation down to the user, requiring application developers to explicitly instrument code (e.g., calling df.count() prior to writes)

  • Optional instrumentation is forgotten instrumentation. In a platform with hundreds of contributors, “every team should remember to do X” is a hope, not a strategy.
  • df.count() isn’t free. It forces an additional materialization pass over the lineage graph unless cached. Now we’re asking every user to think about caching too, which they’ll get wrong.
  • Governance Friction. Two teams tag their metrics differently and we can’t compare them.

Both fail for the same reason: they push observability work onto the platform’s users, instead of making it a property of the platform.


What I Built: The Telemetry Library

The library takes a different approach: it hooks directly into Spark’s runtime internals to collect telemetry as jobs execute—throughput, stage runtimes, GC pauses, memory spill, and task execution profiles.

Integration is a single registration at application startup:

implicit val spark: SparkSession = SparkSession.builder()
 .appName("my-job")
 .getOrCreate()

val observability = new PlatformObservability(
 metricPrefix = "platform.spark.observability",
)(spark)

observability.register()

What does an application team actually get?

  • One line of code. Register once at session initialization; zero pipeline refactoring.
  • Zero compute overhead. Extracted from Spark runtime internals—no trigger queries, no re-computations, no extra cloud spend.
  • Standardized org-wide. Consistent metrics and tags across hundreds of pipelines.

Metrics are pushed asynchronously to a metrics gateway and visualized in Grafana, backing automated anomaly detection and team dashboards.


Beyond Monitoring: Optimization Hints

The library also flags redundant work: if the same DataFrame is recomputed without an intervening .cache() or .persist(), it emits a warning. Catching duplicate compute directly on the dashboard gives engineers immediate actionable items.


The Result: A Real Incident

A daily pipeline once finished completely green—exit code zero, all stages succeeded, alerts silent—but had written only ~40% of its usual rows due to an upstream feed degradation. The data team didn’t catch it; a business user did, hours later, when revenue dashboards dropped.

The library catches that class of silent failure immediately: the moment output volume drops below its rolling baseline, an alert fires before downstream consumers read incomplete data.


Notes: Platform vs. Domain Metrics

The Four Golden Signals answer: Did the pipeline run healthily and efficiently?
They cannot answer: Is the data mathematically and logically correct?

Domain integrity—such as financial reconciliation, or value ranges—still belongs in application-level assertions.


What’s Next

  • Freshness & SLA: Data is landing on time and isn’t stale.
  • Data Quality: Null values, value ranges, referential integrity, etc.
  • Lineage: Shipping captured source/sink metadata to a catalog layer (OpenLineage, Unity Catalog) to map cross-pipeline dependencies.

References

  • Monitoring Distributed Systems — Google SRE Book, Chapter 6 (Four Golden Signals)

item.title: Migrating HDFS to S3 Object Storage with Zero Downtime
item.description:
The Legacy HDFS

A high-throughput backend service (1000+ pods serving live traffic) loaded data from on-prem HDFS. The service reads data into memory at startup and refreshes periodically in the background, while upstream Spark jobs and upload services produce and write the data.


Requirements

The task was to migrate the storage layer from HDFS to S3-compatible object storage. Constraints:

  • Zero downtime
    • Continuous availability with zero maintenance windows.
  • Decoupled lifecycles
    • Independent objects produced by separate upstream pipelines. A single synchronized cutover was not possible.
  • Zero blast radius
    • Live pricing decisions depend on these data. We have to minimize impact as much as possible.

Migration Architecture

Because HDFS reads are off the request path, we used the Strangler pattern with shadow dual-reads without risking service latency. The idea is to implement S3 read behind the existing read interface and used dynamic feature flags to route traffic and perform asynchronous parity diffing per data path.

Dynamic per-path feature flag simplified pseudocode:

enum ReadMode {
 HDFS_ONLY, // Read only from HDFS (instant rollback)
 SHADOW_HDFS, // Read both, compare byte hash, serve HDFS
 SHADOW_S3, // Read both, compare byte hash, serve S3
 S3_ONLY // Read only from S3 (post-cutover)
}

public class StorageReader {
 // ... dependencies: hdfs, s3, config

 public byte[] read(String path) {
 return switch (config.getMode(path)) {
 case HDFS_ONLY -> hdfs.read(path);

 case SHADOW_HDFS -> {
 byte[] data = hdfs.read(path); // serve HDFS
 byte[] shadow = s3.read(path);
 compareAndEmitMetrics(data, shadow);
 yield data;
 }

 case SHADOW_S3 -> {
 byte[] data = s3.read(path); // serve S3
 byte[] shadow = hdfs.read(path);
 compareAndEmitMetrics(data, shadow);
 yield data;
 }

 case S3_ONLY -> s3.read(path);
 };
 }
}

This guarantees:

  • Instant rollback: Switch back to HDFS in seconds via dynamic config—no redeployment.
  • Granular rollout: Migrateper data path.

Migration Phases

1) Plan the Migration

  1. Inventory all data to migrate
  2. Retire obsolete data
  3. Define the migration unit
    • Scope migration per data path rather than per service

2) Build the New Implementation

  1. Consolidate reads behind a single interface
  2. Implement the S3-compatible client
  3. Add per-path dynamic feature flags
    • Toggle per path at runtime without deployments.
  4. Add shadow-read comparison
    • Read from both S3 and HDFS in parallel and emit a metric comparing byte hashes.

3) Upstream Dual-Write

  1. Enable dual-writing across producers
    • Update Spark pipelines and upload services to write to S3 object storage alongside HDFS.

4) Pilot Migration

We migrated a small, representative sample of data across different sizes and read frequencies to test the workflow and uncover issues before full rollout.

  1. Enable the feature flags
    • The service reads from both HDFS and S3, compares byte hashes, and emits diff metrics while still serving verified data.
  2. Monitor parity and the new S3 storage metrics
    • Correctness
      • Byte hash match rate
    • Reliability
      • HTTP 4xx/5xx error rates
      • Connection timeouts and socket drops
      • Client retry counts
    • Performance
      • Latency
      • Throughput

The pilot revealed two operational issues:

  • Large object download timeouts: Downloading large objects caused intermittent drops. We fixed this in Large Object Download.
  • S3 cluster instability during pod boot: The new S3 cluster had transient outages, causing pods to enter CrashLoopBackOff because loading data is required for startup readiness. We fixed this in Failsafe K8s Pod Startup.

5) Migration

With the pilot fixes deployed, we migrated all remaining data in batches.

  1. Roll out remaining paths under shadow validation

6) Cutover

  1. Disable HDFS writes, switch producers to S3-only writes
  2. Turn off HDFS shadow reads
  3. Monitor post-cutover metrics
    • Zero read/write traffic on HDFS
    • S3 storage metrics
    • Application metrics

7) Shutdown

  1. Delete legacy HDFS code & configurations

Large Object Download

During the pilot migration, small objects transferred reliably, but large objects intermittently timed out during pod startup.

Rather than building custom chunked range request logic, we switched to AWS SDK’s native CRT-based S3 client via S3AsyncClient.crtBuilder().


Failsafe K8s Pod Startup

During pilot migration, for some reason S3 storage was unstable which caused pod startup to enter CrashLoopBackOff. To eliminate this single point of failure, we moved the initial data dependency from startup time to build time: a CI step bakes a data snapshot into the Docker image, allowing pods to startup instantly from local disk before polling S3 for asynchronous updates.


References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/strangler-fig.html

item.title: Building an MLOps Velocity Tool
item.description:
ML Pipeline Automation

Google’s MLOps maturity model is a useful starting point. It defines three levels — manual experimentation, partial pipeline automation, and full CI/CD/CT for ML.

These diagrams describe an ideal. Real teams have to decide which parts matter most, and where they’re willing to diverge.

Where Our Team Sits, and Where We Diverged

Our pipeline maps closely to Google’s level 2, but we diverged in two places that mattered:

  1. A custom Velocity Tool, not a generic platform.
    • Ours targets a specific shape of work: an optimization problem where most wins come from iterating on features, not from swapping out model architectures. A data scientist — or a business user with a feature idea — can take a candidate from “SQL in a notebook” to “running in production traffic” without writing pipeline glue.
  2. In-process inference, not a separate serving cluster.
    • Most reference architectures spin up a dedicated model-serving cluster. For our latency budget, that was the wrong trade-off, so inference runs inside the same backend process that serves the request. The price is tighter coupling between the model runtime and the application; the gain is a meaningful latency improvement.

The Velocity Tool

The Velocity Tool reframes model development as a declarative problem. The user describes the experiment they want — a feature, its source, its evaluation context — and the platform handles the rest: data prep, training, backtesting, packaging, and registering the result for review.

Each experiment is a DAG of containerized steps, parameterized by a single spec. Roughly:

experiment:
 feature:
 name: my_new_signal
 source_sql: |
 SELECT entity_id, value
 FROM raw.events
 WHERE event_date = '${datadate}'
 dtype: numeric
 default: 0.0
 base_dataset: weekly_baseline
 evaluation:
 business_metrics: [primary_metric, guardrail_metric]
 backtest_window: 28d
 promotion_policy: requires_human_approval

That’s the entire surface area a user has to learn. Behind it: a Spark feature build, a training step that produces a versioned artifact, an evaluation step enforcing shared business metrics, and lineage captured for audit. Experiments run in parallel, scheduled by the platform.

The Extended Lifecycle: Sandbox and A/B Before Production

A good backtest number means very little on its own. Backtests can lie about live behaviour, and a model can be statistically “better” while still violating a business rule no one wrote down. So the pipeline has two stages between training and production:

  1. Sandbox
    • A model that passed evaluation is replayed against production data, with platform-enforced checks on the output. The point is to fail loudly on what backtests miss — broken feature assumptions, silent regressions on a data segment that matters.
  2. A/B Experimentation
    • Model from the sandbox is then deployed in production, running with a real traffic behind a controlled experiment. The user gets the same business-metric report as in training, now computed against real customer behaviour.

Promotion is a human decision, but its mechanics are fully automated. No “rebuild the artifact for production” step, no rewritten glue code. The artifact that won in A/B is the artifact that runs in production. Removing that gap closes off a long list of “almost the same code, but not quite” bugs.

The Hard Part: Knowing It’s Still Working

Detecting that a deployed model has quietly stopped doing its job is the unsolved problem of MLOps. Three regimes, not equally hard:

  • Labels are direct or cheap. Sample outputs, label them, measure performance. Solvable.
  • Labels are absent or biased. Pick a proxy metric that correlates with what you care about and monitor that — knowing the proxy will eventually drift, and you’ll have to revisit it.
  • The problem is reinforcement-shaped. The model’s own actions change the data it sees, so “compare prediction to ground truth” doesn’t apply. Monitoring becomes distributions, business outcomes, and counterfactuals rather than accuracy.

Most of our production models live in the latter two regimes. A model that sets a price in a live marketplace, for example, never gets to observe what the optimal price would have been — only the outcome at the price it actually showed. The label we want is structurally unobservable, and monitoring this class of system well is one of the challenging problems in MLOps.

Retrospective

Things from building this that I keep coming back to:

  • The spec is the product. The declarative thing a user fills in is the product. The orchestrator, storage layout, and training runtime underneath are implementation details and should be replaceable without breaking that contract.
  • Standardize the workflow The platform has strong opinions about the shape of an experiment — the spec format, the metrics, the promotion path — and stays out of the way of what goes inside it. That trade is what makes it safe for non-engineers to ship without the platform feeling restrictive.
  • Observability belongs inside the pipeline. Lineage, freshness, volume, and distribution drift are first-class outputs of every run, not a separate dashboard you build afterwards.
  • Cost should be visible to whoever decides what to run. A platform that runs hundreds of experiments a week needs to expose per-run cost to its users, not just track it internally.

References

  • MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning — Google Cloud
  • What is MLOps? — AWS

item.title: Pricing Experimentation
item.description:
When we search for products on an e-commerce, the prices are rarely static. Behind the scenes, hundreds of pricing campaigns run at the same time—special mobile app rates, discounts for specific target, or machine learning models adjusting prices.

Before launching a new pricing campaigns to users, we have to test it first: does this campaign actually bring more values?

This is where pricing experimentation comes in.

Unlike a simple frontend A/B test (like testing a new button color or page layout), experimenting with prices happens deep inside backend services on the live search path. We have to evaluate business rules, assign experiment variants, and calculate prices accordinly.


Requirements

Functional Requirements

  • Campaign & Experiment Management
    • An internal UI tool for business teams to create pricing rules, set up A/B tests, and go through an approval process before anything goes live.
  • Targeting (Segmentation)
    • The ability to target specific user groups based on request details (e.g., users browsing on mobile, users searching from a specific country, or logged-in members).
  • Allocation Strategies
    • Support for splitting traffic by different keys (e.g., by user ID, time, etc).
  • Metrics
    • Collecting data on which users saw which prices so we can measure the business impact (conversion rates, revenue, and margins).

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Low Latency
    • Pricing services handle high request volumes. Checking experiment variant cannot add extra long latency.
  • High Availability & Safety
    • The experimentation system must stay available so A/B experiment is not disrupted.

Campaigns, Allocation, Experiment

What each one means:

  1. Campaign: The actual pricing rule or discount logic (for example, “apply a 5% discount”).
  2. Segment: The target audience eligible for that rule (for example, “mobile users searching in Thailand”).
  3. Experiment: The A/B test setup that splits traffic into groups:
    • Control Group (Variant A): Experiences standard pricing behavior (the baseline).
    • Treatment Group (Variant B): Experiences the new pricing campaign.

Because a single experiment might test multiple campaigns, or a campaign might be reused across tests, we keep them in separate tables linked together:

Figure 1: Database schema separating campaign rules, targeting segments, and experiment configurations.

In this setup:

  • The campaign table stores the pricing logic, schedules, and approval statuses.
  • The segment table holds the targeting rules evaluated against incoming search requests.
  • The experiment table links to an allocation strategy that defines how traffic is split.
  • The campaign_experiment table acts as a bridge, mapping which specific campaigns are activated for each variant.

Deterministic Allocation

Once a search request matches a targeted segment, how do we decide whether a user gets Variant A or Variant B? This process is called allocation.

We cannot query a remote database on every search request to look up or store an assignment—that would add too much latency and introduce a single point of failure. Instead, the service computes the variant locally on the fly using deterministic hashing:

$$\text{bucket} = \text{hash}(\text{entity_id}) \pmod{100}$$

At a high level:

  1. We take an identifier like user_id.
  2. We run it through a fast, uniform hash function and map it into a bucket between 0 and 99.
  3. For a 50/50 test, buckets 0–49 get Variant A (Control), and buckets 50–99 get Variant B (Treatment).

Because this is a stateless mathematical calculation, the same user consistently gets the same variant every time they search without storing anything in a database.

When running 100+ of experiments simultaneously, there are some real-world challenges. A classic one is experiment correlation. Solving these requires more advanced allocation techniques.


High-Level Architecture


Integrating Experiments in the Code

When people first think of A/B testing in code, they usually picture a basic if/else check:

request = get_request()
ctx = get_context(request)

# Simple A/B test check
if experiment_client.determine_variant("EXPERIMENT-ID", ctx) == "B":
 plan_b() # Variant B: Treatment
else:
 plan_a() # Variant A: Control

This works well if we only have one or two simple experiments. But in real-world pricing where 100+ of experiments run at the same time across different markets, hardcoding experiment names in code doesn’t work. Every new test would require writing code, testing, and deploying.

Instead, the pricing service uses a rule engine:

request = get_request()
ctx = get_context(request)

# 1. Match request against active campaigns
eligible_campaigns = rule_engine.evaluate(ctx)

# 2. Check experiment variants and apply rules dynamically
for campaign in eligible_campaigns:
 variant = experiment_client.determine_variant(campaign.experiment_id, ctx)
 if variant == "B":
 pricing_calculator.apply_rule(campaign.treatment_rule)
 else:
 pricing_calculator.apply_rule(campaign.control_rule)

With this approach:

  • No deployments needed: Business teams can launch, modify, or stop experiments directly from the internal UI without needing an engineer to deploy code.
  • Handling multiple campaigns: The engine can handle conflict resolution and campaigns stacking.

References

item.title: Detecting Performance Degradation in CI/CD Pipeline
item.description:
Why?

We want to identify any performance degradation before merging code changes into the production environment. Imagine there is a pull request changing some critical logic in the code in a way that increases latency of a backend service by a lot, and this is detected after deployed to the production!


The Testing Setup

So the basic idea of performance regresssion test is to compare the performance between 2 instances of a backend application; 1 from the baseline (curerntly in production build) and another from the candidate build triggered by a pull request (PR) or a merge request (MR).

We also want to ensure the fairness of the test, so the baseline and the candidate versions will be deployed in isolated environment. For this, Kubernetes CPU Limit can be used.

We can also use tools like k6 to run the performance test.


The .gitlab-ci.yml


stages:
 # ...
 - docker
 - manual
 # ...

app_docker:
 stage: docker
 script:
 # Build docker image
 artifacts:
 paths:
 # ...

performance_regression_test:
 stage: manual
 extends:
 # ...
 allow_failure: true
 needs:
 - job: app_docker
 variables:
 # ...
 trigger:
 include:
 - local: .ci/pipelinees/performance_test/pipeline.yaml
 strategy: depend
 resource_group: # ...

# .ci/pipelinees/performance_test/pipeline.yaml

stages:
 - test setup # Prepare sample requests, build test runner, deploy baseline & candidate to Kubernetes
 - perf test # Run the perf test by firing requests to the baseline & candidate
 - cleanup # Clean up the Kubernetes resource
 - analyze # Analyze the result, 

workflow:
 rules:
 - if: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID
 - if: $CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

deploy_baseline:
 stage: test setup
 # ...

deploy_candidate:
 stage: test setup
 # ...

perf_test_baseline:
 stage: perf test
 # ...

perf_test_candidate:
 stage: perf test
 # ...

cleanup_baseline:
 stage: cleanup
 # ...

cleanup_candidate:
 stage: cleanup
 # ...

analyze_result:
 stage: analyze
 script:
 # Analyze the result

References

  • https://grafana.com/blog/2021/01/27/k6-vs-jmeter-comparison/
